title: Taking the GP Out of the Loop
claim: Surrogate-based methods slow superlinearly as observations grow; ours stays near zero and scales linearly, beating every baseline.
layout: 2x2 scatter grid, shared legend at bottom, last panel zoomed
description: Four scatter-plot panels in a 2x2 grid show proposal time in seconds (y-axis) against number of observations N (x-axis). Panels (a), (b) and (c) use D = 100, 300 and 1000. Panel (d) is a zoomed view of D = 1000. Seven methods appear as different colored markers: blue circles for ucb:sparse, orange crosses for ucb, green triangles for turbo-one, red dots for vecchia, purple squares for optuna and bold gray rings for turbo-enn. A shared legend sits below the panels. In (a), ucb:sparse shoots up to about 100 s while the others stay near zero. In (b) and (c), ucb, vecchia and turbo-one climb steeply. Optuna rises slowly. Turbo-enn hugs the zero line in all three. The zoom in (d) shows turbo-enn rising linearly from about 0.17 s to 0.5 s. The eye goes first to the high outlier markers.
caption: Mean proposal time (in seconds) versus number of observations ($N$) for several Bayesian optimization methods. We set $N = D$ in these runs. Subfigures show results for (a) $D = 100$, (b) $D = 300$, (c) $D = 1000$, and (d) a zoomed-in view of (c), averaged over many optimization runs (see Section [ref]). GP-based methods (ucb and turbo-one) scale approximately as $O(N^2)$, while optuna, which uses a Parzen estimator, vecchia, a nearest-neighbor GP method, and our method (turbo-enn) scale linearly in $N$. Scaling behavior for ucb:sparse, which uses a sparse GP, is not simple. Results are averaged over 12 functions $\times$ 10 BO runs/function = 120 runs for each optimization method. The functions, \{ackley, rastrigin, sphere, trid, booth, mccormick, dixonprice, rosenbrock, dejong5, easom, branin, stybtang\}, consist of two functions each from the six categories of optimizer test function in [ref]. The various methods are discussed in more detail in Section [ref].
abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) has traditionally solved black-box problems where function evaluation is expensive and, therefore, observations are few. Recently, however, there has been growing interest in applying BO to problems where function evaluation is cheaper and observations are more plentiful. In this regime, scaling to many observations $N$ is impeded by Gaussian-process (GP) surrogates: GP hyperparameter fitting scales as $\mathcal{O}(N^3)$ (reduced to roughly $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ in modern implementations), and it is repeated at every BO iteration. Many methods improve scaling at acquisition time, but hyperparameter fitting still scales poorly, making it the bottleneck. We propose Epistemic Nearest Neighbors (ENN), a lightweight alternative to GPs that estimates function values and uncertainty (epistemic and aleatoric) from $K$-nearest-neighbor observations. ENN scales as $\mathcal{O}(N)$ for both fitting and acquisition. Our BO method, TuRBO-ENN, replaces the GP surrogate in TuRBO with ENN and its Thompson-sampling acquisition with $\mathrm{UCB} = Î¼(x) + Ï(x)$. For the special case of noise-free problems, we can omit fitting altogether by replacing $\mathrm{UCB}$ with a non-dominated sort over $Î¼(x)$ and $Ï(x)$. We show empirically that TuRBO-ENN reduces proposal time (i.e., fitting time + acquisition time) by one to two orders of magnitude compared to TuRBO at up to 50,000 observations.
